newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African truce extended for one month.
newsitem.headline: Central African truce extended for one month.

text.p: The Central African Republic government and army mutineers on Sunday extended for one month a ceasefire in the capital Bangui and agreed to form a joint security commission, a presidential spokesman said.
Thousands of Bangui residents had fled the capital ahead of the Sunday expiration date of the previous 15-day ceasefire brokered by four African presidents.
A third of the city's population of 600,000 has left according to some estimates.
The ceasefire will now stay in place until January 23, during which time rebels and loyalist troops would maintain positions, spokesman Theophile Doumbe told Reuters.
"A joint security commission was established comprising 10 members -- five from the loayalist forces and five from the rebel forces," Doumbe said.
Both sides agreed to refrain from any acts or statements likely to compromise national unity during the truce period.

The accord was signed by President Ange-Felix Patasse, rebel leader Captain Anicet Saulet, mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure, the former military ruler of Mali, and French ambassador Jean-Marc Simon, who took part in the negotiations.
Doumbe said authorities also agreed to implement the night curfew at midnight instead of three hours earlier as previously in place.

French troops based in the former colony under bilateral accords helped keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power during a violent mutiny last May and have been backing loyalist forces in the latest revolt.

Mutineers with pay grievances later started demanding that Patasse step down. Patasse was elected 1993 and has dismissed calls for his resignation, backed by the opposition, as unconstitutional. The mutiny has turned into bloody feuding between his Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate the ranks of rebel soldiers.
Soldiers accuse Patasse of arming his civilian supporters and of hiring mercenaries from Chad and Sudan. The rebels have vowed to forcibly disarm Patasse loyalists, stoking tension.
The two principal roads leading out of Bangui have been choked with residents heading to their home provinces in buses, trucks and whatever other means. Some are forced to walk.

"My house has just been destroyed by the military. What I want to do now is leave Bangui forever. I have never seen such violence in 40 years," said Daniel Demba, loading his belongings on a truck at the Kilometre Five motor park.
Several houses have been hit in the cross-fire of rocket propelled grenades in battles between the two sides.

Soldiers had revolted in April and May over pay and status. French troops using helicopter gunships and armoured vehicles clashed with rebels in May before Patasse agreed on concessions that ended the uprising for a period.
